seo.shortDescription: U.S. import duty on all 30 HTS Chapter 97 lines: paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps, coins, collectors' pieces and antiques are Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. China pays 7.5%, Canada 50% on 16 lines, Russia 35%. Plus cultural property, ivory and antique rules.

overview.intro:
Chapter 97 covers works of art and collectibles: paintings, drawings and pastels executed by hand, collages and mosaics (9701), original prints (9702), original sculptures (9703), used and collectible stamps (9704), collections and collectors' pieces such as archaeological and ethnographic objects, fossils, minerals and coins (9705), and antiques over 100 years old (9706). The U.S. imported **$9.98B** of these goods in 2025, 29% from France. **All 30 lines are Free** at the general rate.

Most countries pay nothing extra: every Chapter 97 line is on the **general exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 duties** (U.S. note 52(b)) and on **Brazil's exemption list**, so a painting or antique from France, the UK, Switzerland, Germany, Italy or Hong Kong enters Free. Three measures do charge: **China** pays the 7.5% Section 301 List 4A duty on every line, **Canada** pays the 50% **Section 338** duty on 11 subheadings (paintings and drawings, recent original prints, sculptures, stamps, most collectors' pieces and antiques 100–250 years old), even with a USMCA claim, and **Russia** pays 35% in place of the column 2 rate.

The 2025–2026 emergency tariffs ended: IEEPA on February 24, 2026 and the Section 122 surcharge on July 23, 2026. Both excepted art, stamps and collectors' pieces as **informational materials** (50 U.S.C. 1702(b)(3), the "Berman Amendment"), but **antiques (9706) paid them**. The duty is rarely the hard part: **cultural property** import restrictions (CPIA bilateral agreements and emergency actions, plus Iraq and Syria), **ivory** and other endangered-species rules, and proof of age and authorship decide whether an object can enter. See Tariff engineering.

productGroups.label: Paintings, drawings, pastels, collages & mosaics (executed by hand)
productGroups.blurb: Oil, acrylic and watercolor paintings, drawings and pastels executed entirely by hand, plus collages, mosaics and similar decorative plaques: 6 lines, split by age (over 100 years: 9701.21–.29; other: 9701.91–.99). All Free. Frames of a normal kind and value go with the picture (note 6). Hand-painted manufactured articles, technical drawings of heading 4906 and mass-produced mosaics (note 2) are classified elsewhere.

productGroups.label: Original engravings, prints & lithographs
productGroups.blurb: Impressions printed directly from plates, stones or blocks wholly executed by hand by the artist (note 3): etchings, engravings, woodcuts, lithographs and screenprints, over 100 years old (9702.10) or not (9702.90). Free. Photomechanical reproductions and posters are printed matter of heading 4911.

productGroups.label: Original sculptures & statuary, in any material
productGroups.blurb: Original sculptures and statuary in any material, over 100 years old (9703.10) or not (9703.90), including the first 12 castings, replicas or reproductions made from the sculptor's original model (additional U.S. note 1). Free. Mass-produced reproductions and works of conventional craftsmanship of a commercial character are excluded (note 4) and classified by material.

productGroups.label: Postage & revenue stamps, first-day covers, postal stationery
productGroups.blurb: Used stamps and unused stamps that are not of current or new issue in the country where they have face value, stamp-postmarks, first-day covers and postal stationery: one Free line (9704.00.00). Unused current-issue stamps are heading 4907.

productGroups.label: Collections & collectors' pieces: archaeological, ethnographic, natural history, coins
productGroups.blurb: Collections and collectors' pieces of archaeological, ethnographic or historical interest (9705.10, with statistical lines for archaeological pieces at least 250 years old and ethnographic pieces), of zoological, botanical, mineralogical, anatomical or paleontological interest (9705.21–.29: human specimens, extinct or endangered species, fossils, minerals), and of numismatic interest (9705.31 over 100 years old, 9705.39 other; gold and other coins). All Free.

productGroups.label: Antiques over 100 years old
productGroups.blurb: Antiques of an age exceeding 100 years that are not covered by 9701–9705 (note 5(b)): over 250 years (9706.10) or 100 to 250 years (9706.90), each split into silverware, furniture and other. Free, but an article entered for sale as an antique and later found to be under 100 years old pays its normal rate plus 6.6% (additional U.S. note 2).

workedExamples.title: A $2 million 19th-century oil painting from the United Kingdom
workedExamples.body: Paintings executed entirely by hand and over 100 years old are 9701.21, **Free**. The UK's 10% 2026 Section 301 duty does not apply because the line is on the note 52(b) exemption list (report 9903.05.86). The only charge is the **merchandise processing fee**: 0.3464% of value, capped at **$670.86** per entry from October 1, 2026. Invoice the artist and title; CBP can ask for proof the work is an original (19 CFR 10.48).

workedExamples.title: A French commode from about 1850
workedExamples.body: Antique furniture 100 to 250 years old is 9706.90.00.40, **Free** today. It paid the 10% reciprocal duty from April 5, 2025, the EU's **15%** all-in rate from August 7, 2025, and the **10% Section 122** surcharge from February 24 to July 23, 2026, because antiques are not informational materials. Keep proof of age: if CBP finds a piece entered for sale as an antique is under 100 years old, it pays the furniture rate **plus 6.6%** (additional U.S. note 2), and an upholstered wooden seat could also face the 15% Section 232 wood duty for EU goods.

workedExamples.title: A contemporary bronze sculpture from Canada
workedExamples.body: Original sculptures not over 100 years old are 9703.90, Free at the general rate, but 9703.90 is on the Canada **Section 338** list (U.S. note 51(b)(3)), so since August 22, 2026 a $100,000 sculpture pays **50%: $50,000**, even if it qualifies for USMCA. A sculpture over 100 years old (9703.10) is on the list too. The duty does not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98, such as a work brought in temporarily under bond for exhibition (9813.00.70), or to personal-use goods in accompanied baggage.

workedExamples.title: A Qing dynasty porcelain vase from China
workedExamples.body: An antique over 250 years old is 9706.10.00.60. China pays the **7.5%** Section 301 List 4A duty (9903.88.15) on every Chapter 97 line, so a $40,000 vase pays **$3,000**; the List 4A product exclusions once granted for antiques have expired. In 2025 it also paid the IEEPA fentanyl and reciprocal duties (up to 145% in April–May 2025). The U.S.–China cultural property agreement restricts archaeological material through the Tang period (A.D. 907) and monumental sculpture and wall art at least 250 years old, so a Qing vase is not designated, but a Tang tomb figure needs a Chinese export permit or proof it left China before January 14, 2009.

workedExamples.title: An ancient Roman silver coin bought from a dealer in Germany
workedExamples.body: Coins over 100 years old are 9705.31 (coins made before the 14th century and not known to come from excavations report 9705.31.00.01), **Free** from Germany. "Coins of Italian types" are on the designated list under the U.S.–Italy cultural property agreement (extended through January 12, 2031), so a coin of such a type needs an Italian export certificate or evidence under 19 CFR 12.104c that it left Italy before it was designated or at least 10 years before entry. Without it, CBP can seize it.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) unused postage or revenue stamps, postal stationery or the like, of heading 4907; (b) theatrical scenery, studio backdrops or the like, of painted canvas (heading 5907) except if they may be classified in heading 9706; or (c) pearls, natural or cultured, or precious or semiprecious stones (headings 7101 to 7103).

**Note 2.** Heading 9701 does not apply to mosaics that are mass-produced reproductions, casts or works of conventional craftsmanship of a commercial character, even if these articles are designed or created by artists.

**Note 3.** For heading 9702, "original engravings, prints and lithographs" means impressions produced directly, in black and white or in color, of one or of several plates wholly executed by hand by the artist, irrespective of the process or of the material employed, but not including any mechanical or photomechanical process.

**Note 4.** Heading 9703 does not apply to mass-produced reproductions or works of conventional craftsmanship of a commercial character, even if these articles are designed or created by artists.

**Note 5.** (a) Subject to notes 1 to 4, articles of this chapter are to be classified in this chapter and not in any other chapter. (b) Heading 9706 does not apply to articles of the preceding headings of this chapter.

**Note 6.** Frames around paintings, drawings, pastels, collages or similar decorative plaques, engravings, prints or lithographs are classified with those articles if they are of a kind and of a value normal to those articles; other frames are classified separately.

**Statistical notes.** For 9705.10.00.10, "archaeological pieces" are objects of cultural significance at least 250 years old of a kind normally discovered by scientific excavation, clandestine or accidental digging or exploration on land or under water; for 9705.10.00.20, "ethnographic pieces" are products of a tribal or nonindustrial society important to the cultural heritage of a people. Collections mixing several kinds of cultural property are reported by their separate components.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Heading 9703 covers not only original sculpture made by the sculptor, but also the first 12 castings, replicas or reproductions made from a sculptor's original work or model, by the sculptor or by another artist, with or without a change in scale and whether or not the sculptor is alive when they are completed.

**2.** Whenever an article is entered for sale under heading 9706 and is then found to be not over 100 years old, an additional duty of 6.6% ad valorem (column 1), free for goods originating in Canada, or 25% (column 2) is assessed, on top of any other duty or penalty.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 97 Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Art, Antiques & Collectibles

seo.title: Art & Antiques Tariff Updates 2025–2026: IEEPA, Section 122, Section 301, Canada 338 (HTS Ch. 97) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. imports of art, antiques, coins and stamps since January 2025: the informational-materials exemption, IEEPA and Section 122 duties on antiques and their end, the 2026 Section 301 exemption, Canada's 50% Section 338 duty, China List 4A and new cultural property restrictions, with official citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 30 Chapter 97 lines were Free in both, and still are.

The extra duties split the chapter in two. Paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps and collectors' pieces (**9701–9705**) are **informational materials**, which IEEPA cannot regulate (50 U.S.C. 1702(b)(3)), so they were excepted from every 2025 IEEPA duty and from the 2026 Section 122 surcharge. **Antiques (9706)** were not: they paid 25% (35% from August 1) on non-USMCA goods of Canada, 25% on Mexico, the fentanyl and reciprocal duties on China and Hong Kong, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else (10%, then country rates from August 7, 2025 such as 15% all-in for the EU, 39% for Switzerland until November 14, 2025, 10% for the UK) and 50% on Brazil. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% **Section 122** surcharge, charged on antiques only, expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today three measures charge Chapter 97 goods: China's **Section 301 List 4A** duty of 7.5% on all 30 lines (continued by USTR on October 7, 2026), the 50% **Section 338** duty on 16 lines from **Canada** (from August 22, 2026, USMCA or not), and Russia's 35% rate. The **2026 Section 301** duties on 60 economies and **Brazil's** 25% duty exempt the whole chapter. Cultural property restrictions kept growing, with new agreements with India (2025) and Nepal (2026) and emergency restrictions for Lebanon (2025).
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 97 from any country (China Section 301 List 4A, Canada Section 338, Russia; the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties and their exemptions; the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties), plus cultural property restrictions published by CBP and the State Department and the FWS ivory rule. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 97 goods. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: The 50% duty (9903.03.14, U.S. note 51(b)(3), Proclamation 11048) applies from August 22, 2026 whether or not USMCA is claimed, with no informational-materials exception. It does not apply to personal-use goods in accompanied baggage or to goods properly entered under Chapter 98 (with exceptions such as the 9802 repair and assembly provisions), such as works brought in temporarily under bond. The September 15, 2026 changes (Proclamation 11065) did not touch the Chapter 97 subheadings. The 2025 IEEPA duty on Canada excepted 9701–9705 (9903.01.12) and charged non-USMCA antiques; it ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Canadian paintings, drawings and other works under 100 years old (9701.91, 9701.99) and paintings over 100 years old (9701.21), original prints not over 100 years old, all original sculptures, stamps, collectors' pieces of historical, natural-history and numismatic interest (9705.10, 9705.29, 9705.39) and antiques 100–250 years old (9706.90) pay 50%. Mosaics, other 9701.2x works over 100 years, old prints, human and endangered-species specimens, coins over 100 years old and antiques over 250 years old stay Free.

inEffect.exemption: The 7.5% List 4A duty (9903.88.15, U.S. note 20(r)–(s)) covers all 30 Chapter 97 lines. The List 4A product exclusions USTR granted for paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps, some collectors' pieces and antique silverware, furniture and other antiques (note 20(ddd) and (fff), 9903.88.51/.53) have expired. There is no informational-materials exception from Section 301. Hong Kong-origin goods are not products of China for this duty. The 2026 Section 301 duty (12.5%) does not apply: every Chapter 97 line is on note 52(b). The IEEPA duties on China and Hong Kong, which excepted 9701–9705 but charged antiques, ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Every Chinese work of art, stamp, coin, collectors' piece and antique pays 7.5% (Free + 7.5%); a $100,000 Chinese painting pays $7,500.

inEffect.exemption: Russia has paid column 2 rates since April 2022 (Pub. L. 117-110); Proclamation 10420 put all of Chapter 97 on the U.S. note 30(b) list, which sets 35% in place of the Free column 2 rate (9903.90.08). There is no informational-materials exception. The 2026 Section 301 duty on Russia does not apply (note 52(b)). Goods entered under Chapter 98 (with exceptions such as the 9802 repair and assembly provisions) are not charged.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Russian paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps, coins, collectors' pieces and antiques pay 35% instead of Free.

changes.title: Chapter 97 base rates: no changes, all Free
changes.detail: All 30 Chapter 97 tariff lines carry the same General (Free), Special and Column 2 (Free) rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition.

changes.title: China Section 301 actions continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the Section 301 actions on China, including the 7.5% List 4A duty on all 30 Chapter 97 lines, continue while the review proceeds. No Chapter 97 product exclusion is in effect.

changes.title: Cultural Property Advisory Committee to review Cyprus, Guatemala and Peru agreements
changes.detail: The State Department called a Cultural Property Advisory Committee meeting for October 27–29, 2026 to review proposed extensions of the bilateral cultural property agreements with Cyprus, Guatemala and Peru. Their import restrictions on designated archaeological and ethnological material stay in force while the extensions are considered.

changes.title: Canada Section 338: 50% on 16 Chapter 97 lines
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 imposed a 50% duty on products of Canada in the provisions listed in U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14), applied from August 22, 2026 (Proclamation 11056). The list names 9701.21, 9701.91, 9701.99, 9702.90, 9703.10, 9703.90, 9704.00, 9705.10, 9705.29, 9705.39 and 9706.90. The duty applies even to USMCA-qualifying goods and has no informational-materials exception. The September 15, 2026 changes (Proclamation 11065) left these subheadings unchanged.

changes.title: New cultural property restrictions: Nepal
changes.detail: CBP added Nepal to the bilateral agreements in 19 CFR 12.104g: designated archaeological material from 32,000 B.C.E. through 1770 C.E. and ethnological material from the 13th century through 1950 C.E. need a Nepalese export certificate or proof under 19 CFR 12.104c, through January 8, 2031.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies: Chapter 97 exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect, but every Chapter 97 line is on the general exemption list in U.S. note 52(b), so works of art, collectibles and antiques from the UK, the EU, Switzerland, Japan, India and the other listed economies pay nothing extra (report 9903.05.86). The separate informational-materials heading (9903.05.92) covers 9701–9705 too, but is not needed for this chapter.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It had charged antiques (9706) from every country except USMCA goods; works of art and collectibles (9701–9705) were excepted as informational materials (9903.03.11).

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: Chapter 97 exempt
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect, but every Chapter 97 line is on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03), so Brazilian art and antiques stay Free.

changes.title: De minimis suspension made indefinite
changes.detail: The $800 duty-free de minimis exemption has been suspended for all countries since August 29, 2025 (Executive Order 14324), kept after the IEEPA ruling (Executive Order 14388), and suspended indefinitely for all modes other than the postal network by CBP's interim final rule of June 24, 2026. Low-value parcels of stamps, coins and small collectibles need an entry, and Chinese ones pay the 7.5% List 4A duty.

changes.title: Türkiye cultural property restrictions extended to 2031
changes.detail: CBP extended the import restrictions on designated archaeological material of Türkiye (about 1,200,000 B.C. to A.D. 1770) and ethnological material (1st century to 1923) through March 24, 2031.

changes.title: Afghanistan emergency restrictions extended to 2029
changes.detail: CBP extended the emergency import restrictions on archaeological material of Afghanistan (50,000 B.C. through A.D. 1747) and ethnological material (9th century through 1920) through April 28, 2029.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge on antiques; art excepted
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Works of art, stamps and collectors' pieces (9701–9705) were excepted as informational materials (9903.03.11); antiques (9706) paid it unless entered under USMCA (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. In Chapter 97 they had charged only antiques (9706).

changes.title: Italy cultural property restrictions extended to 2031
changes.detail: CBP extended the import restrictions on designated pre-Classical, Classical and Imperial Roman archaeological material of Italy, including "coins of Italian types", through January 12, 2031.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 97 line: this duty has no Chapter 97 exemption. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Switzerland: reciprocal rate cut to 15% all-in
changes.detail: The U.S.–Switzerland–Liechtenstein framework replaced the 39% reciprocal duty with the higher of the base rate or 15%, for goods entered from November 14, 2025. Swiss antiques paid 15% until February 24, 2026; art was excepted.

changes.title: De minimis exemption suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free entry for shipments valued at $800 or less from every country, effective for goods entered from August 29, 2025.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates on antiques
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates, for example 15% all-in for the EU and Japan, 39% for Switzerland, 25% for India and 10% for the United Kingdom. In Chapter 97 only antiques (9706) paid them; India's antiques also paid the additional 25% of Executive Order 14329 from August 27, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty on antiques
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added a 40% duty on products of Brazil (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Informational materials, including 9701–9705, were excepted (9903.01.80); Brazilian antiques paid 50%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Art and collectibles were excepted (9903.01.12); non-USMCA antiques paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: New cultural property restrictions: India
changes.detail: CBP added India to 19 CFR 12.104g: designated archaeological material (about 1.7 million years ago to 1770 C.E.) and ethnological material (2nd century B.C.E. to 1947 C.E.) need an Indian export certificate or proof under 19 CFR 12.104c, through July 26, 2029.

changes.title: China IEEPA duties: reciprocal rate cut to 10%
changes.detail: Chinese and Hong Kong antiques paid IEEPA duties on top of Section 301: a fentanyl-related 10% from February 4, 2025 (20% from March 4, back to 10% from November 10, 2025) and a reciprocal duty that rose to 125% in April 2025 and was cut to 10% from May 14, 2025. Art and collectibles of 9701–9705 were excepted as informational materials (9903.01.22, 9903.01.31) and paid only the 7.5% List 4A duty. All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Emergency cultural property restrictions: Lebanon
changes.detail: CBP imposed emergency import restrictions on designated archaeological material of Lebanon (Paleolithic to 1774 C.E.) and ethnological material (1600 to 1918 C.E.), in effect until January 23, 2029 unless extended.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: 10% on antiques, art excepted
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025. IEEPA cannot regulate informational materials (50 U.S.C. 1702(b)(3)), so paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps and collectors' pieces were entered free of it under 9903.01.31; CBP's guidance lists 9701–9705 among the goods that may qualify. Antiques (9706) paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025. Informational materials, including art and collectibles of 9701–9705, were excepted (9903.01.12, 9903.01.03); antiques paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Emergency cultural property restrictions: Ukraine
changes.detail: CBP imposed emergency import restrictions on designated archaeological material of Ukraine (Paleolithic through 1774 C.E.) and ethnological material (200 to 1917 C.E.), in effect until March 5, 2029 unless extended.

changes.title: China cultural property restrictions extended to 2029
changes.detail: CBP extended the import restrictions on Chinese archaeological material from the Paleolithic through the end of the Tang period (A.D. 907) and on monumental sculpture and wall art at least 250 years old, through January 14, 2029.

changes.title: Russia: 35% on all Chapter 97 goods
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set a 35% rate in place of the column 2 rate for the products of Russia listed in U.S. note 30(b) (9903.90.08), including every Chapter 97 subheading. Russian art and antiques had been Free at column 2.

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: USTR halved the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5%. List 4A took effect September 1, 2019 and covers every Chapter 97 subheading. USTR later granted product exclusions for paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps, some collectors' pieces and antiques; they have since expired (U.S. note 20(ddd), (fff)).

changes.title: Syria: emergency restrictions on cultural property
changes.detail: Under the Protect and Preserve International Cultural Property Act, CBP restricted imports of archaeological and ethnological material unlawfully removed from Syria on or after March 15, 2011 (19 CFR 12.104k).

changes.title: African elephant ivory: commercial imports banned, antiques excepted
changes.detail: The FWS revision of the African elephant 4(d) rule took effect: worked ivory may not be imported except in limited non-commercial cases (musical instruments, traveling exhibitions, household moves and inheritances), while antiques meeting the Endangered Species Act test (at least 100 years old, not repaired with endangered species parts since December 28, 1973, imported through an antique port) remain importable.

changes.title: Iraq: restrictions on cultural property
changes.detail: Under the Emergency Protection for Iraqi Cultural Antiquities Act of 2004, CBP restricted imports of archaeological and ethnological material illegally removed from Iraq since UN Security Council Resolution 661 of August 6, 1990 (19 CFR 12.104j).

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 97 goods were **$9.98B in 2025**, up 12.2% from $8.9B in 2024; the 2020–2025 peak was $10.46B in 2023. U.S. import statistics record the country of origin, where the work was made, not where it was bought. The largest suppliers were **France** $2.87B (29%, up 24.9%), **United Kingdom** $1.63B (16%, down 1.8%), **Italy** $1.09B (11%, up 2.6%), **Germany** $1.03B (10%, up 5.2%), **Spain** $547M (6%, up 97.1%), **Belgium** $525M (5%, up 33.3%). Together the EU and the UK supply most of the chapter, and all of it enters Free today.

By product, paintings dominate: paintings, drawings and pastels not over 100 years old (9701.91) $5.06B; paintings, drawings and pastels over 100 years old (9701.21) $2.2B; original sculptures not over 100 years old (9703.90) $1.38B; antiques 100 to 250 years old (9706.90) $278M. Paintings, drawings and other works of 9701 rose 22% to $7.43B, while **antiques (9706) fell 49%** to $416M: in 2025 antiques were the only Chapter 97 goods that paid the IEEPA duties, since works of art and collectibles (9701–9705) entered free of them as informational materials.

The extra duties that remain fall on small suppliers: **Canada** ($131M, now 50% on 16 lines), **China** ($79M, down 26.7%, 7.5%) and **Russia**, whose shipments fell from $31.4M in 2020 to $794K in 2025 after the 35% rate took effect in July 2022. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so it shows neither the 2026 Section 301 exemption nor Canada's Section 338 duty. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Every Chapter 97 line is Free, so each cell is **the extra duty for the country of origin**, computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator. For most countries it is zero: the **2026 Section 301** duties exempt the whole chapter (note 52(b)), and so does **Brazil's** 25% duty (note 50(a)(ii)).

Cells for 9701–9705 show a second total, "Free if informational materials" (the breakdown reads "not informational materials / informational materials"). The calculator asks whether the goods are **informational materials** (9903.05.92, 9903.05.09), because that claim lifts the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties on 9701–9705. Here both answers give Free, because note 52(b) already exempts every line, including antiques, which are not informational materials. Three origins differ: **China** pays 7.5% on everything, **Canada** 50% on 16 of 30 lines whether or not USMCA is claimed, and **Russia** 35%. None of the three has an informational-materials exception.

tariffEngineering.h1: Importing Art, Antiques & Collectibles (HTS Ch. 97): Cultural Property, Ivory, Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Art & Antiques into the U.S.: Cultural Property Rules, Ivory, Proof of Age and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 97) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariff engineering and entry rules for HTS Chapter 97: classifying originals vs reproductions and antiques, proof of age, country of origin, Chapter 98 temporary entry for exhibitions, the merchandise processing fee, plus CPIA cultural property restrictions, Iraq and Syria, pre-Columbian sculpture, and the ivory and endangered-species rules for antiques.
keywords: can you import ivory into the us

tariffEngineering.intro:
Chapter 97 goods are Free at the general rate, so the levers are about **staying in Chapter 97** and **avoiding the three extra duties** (China 7.5%, Canada 50% on 16 lines, Russia 35%). An object that is a reproduction, a work of conventional craftsmanship or under 100 years old belongs in another chapter, where it pays that chapter's rate and, for most origins, the 2026 Section 301 duty that Chapter 97 escapes. Proof of authorship and age, the right country of origin and Chapter 98 temporary-entry provisions do the rest.

The bigger risk is not duty but **seizure**. Designated archaeological and ethnological material from the 30-plus countries with U.S. cultural property agreements or emergency actions needs export documents; material illegally removed from Iraq or Syria is restricted; stolen inventory of foreign museums and pre-Columbian monumental sculpture cannot enter; and **elephant ivory** and other endangered-species parts may enter only as qualifying antiques through designated ports. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Classify as an original work, collectors' piece or antique, not a decorative article or reproduction
levers.saves: The other chapter's base rate plus, for most origins, the 2026 Section 301 duty that note 52(b) lifts only for Chapter 97: for example 3.3% + 10% on modern French sterling tableware (7114.11.50) vs Free as antique silverware over 100 years old; a 1950s EU upholstered wooden chair pays 15% Section 232 (9903.76.22) vs Free as a 9706 antique
levers.appliesTo: Paintings vs hand-painted articles, original prints vs photomechanical reproductions (4911), sculptures vs mass-produced statuettes (chapters 44, 69, 83), antiques vs newer furniture, silverware and decorative goods
levers.document: An invoice naming the artist and stating whether each work is an original, a replica or a copy; for sculpture, that it is the original or one of the first 12 castings (additional U.S. note 1); for prints, that they were printed by hand from hand-made plates (19 CFR 10.48). Normal frames go with the picture (note 6). A binding ruling under 19 CFR part 177 settles a close case before import.
levers.caveat: Notes 2 and 4 exclude mass-produced reproductions and works of conventional craftsmanship of a commercial character, even when designed by an artist. Classification follows what the object is; describing décor as art is false classification.

citations.label: CBP ICP: Works of Art, Collector's Pieces, Antiques

levers.title: Prove an antique is over 100 years old (or over 250, which matters for Canada)
levers.saves: Avoids the extra 6.6% that additional U.S. note 2 adds when an article entered for sale as an antique turns out to be under 100 years old, on top of its normal rate; for Canada, an antique over 250 years old (9706.10) is off the Section 338 list while 9706.90 pays 50%
levers.appliesTo: Antiques of 9706, and the age splits in 9701, 9702, 9703 and 9705.31
levers.document: Evidence of age: dealer or auction invoices describing the period, expert appraisals, provenance and photographs (19 CFR 10.53). A repaired antique stays Free; substantial added material is appraised and dutiable separately, and an object altered beyond its original identity loses free entry (19 CFR 10.53(b)).
levers.caveat: The 6.6% is waived if the article was not imported for sale or the antique claim is withdrawn in writing before examination (19 CFR 10.53(f)–(g)).

levers.title: Declare the right country of origin: where the work was made
levers.saves: The extra duties attach to origin, not to where the work was bought: a Chinese painting bought at auction in London or Hong Kong still pays China's 7.5%; a French antique bought in Canada pays no Section 338 duty
levers.appliesTo: All lines; matters for goods made in China, Canada or Russia
levers.document: Provenance showing where the object was made; the country of origin is the country of manufacture or production (19 CFR 134.1(b)). Articles produced more than 20 years before import, such as antiques, and stamps (J-list) are exempt from origin marking, but the entry must still state the origin.
levers.caveat: Re-framing, restoring or reselling a work abroad does not change its origin. Mis-declaring origin is fraud.

levers.title: Use Chapter 98 for exhibitions, artists' works on tour and works returning to the United States
levers.saves: Free entry with no Canada Section 338 or Russia 35% duty (both notes exempt goods properly entered under Chapter 98, with exceptions such as the 9802 repair and assembly provisions) and no merchandise processing fee (19 CFR 24.23(c)(1)(i))
levers.appliesTo: Works lent to museums and fairs, works brought in by visiting artists, and U.S. works returning after exhibition or sale attempts abroad
levers.document: Temporary importation under bond for works of the free fine arts brought in by professional artists for exhibition (9813.00.70) or articles for exhibition by institutions established for the encouragement of the arts (9812.00.20), with a TIB or ATA Carnet (19 CFR 10.31, part 114); or proof of U.S. origin for American goods returned (9801.00.10, 19 CFR 10.1).
levers.caveat: Bonded goods must be exported within the bond period or the duties and fees become due. Chapter 98 does not lift cultural property, ivory or other entry restrictions.

levers.title: Carry personal-use items from Canada in accompanied baggage
levers.saves: The 50% Section 338 duty, which does not apply to products for personal use in the accompanied baggage of persons arriving in the United States (U.S. note 51(a))
levers.appliesTo: Canadian paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps and collectibles of the 16 listed lines bought for personal use
levers.document: Declare the goods on arrival as personal effects (19 CFR part 148).
levers.caveat: Commercial quantities, goods for sale and shipped goods do not qualify.

levers.title: Claim drawback when dutiable works are re-exported
levers.saves: Generally 99% of the China List 4A, Canada Section 338 or Russia duties paid, on goods re-exported unused (for example a work consigned to a U.S. sale and sent back unsold)
levers.appliesTo: Chinese, Canadian (listed lines) and Russian goods
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with the import and export records (19 CFR part 191); the claim is generally 99% of the eligible duties (19 CFR 191.51).
levers.caveat: Claims must be filed within five years of import, and the export must be documented.

rules.title: Cultural property agreements and emergency actions (CPIA): designated archaeological or ethnological material of a country listed in 19 CFR 12.104g (bilateral agreements with about 30 countries, among them China, Italy, Greece, Egypt, Peru, Türkiye, India and Nepal, and emergency actions for Afghanistan, Lebanon and Ukraine) may enter only with the country's export certificate, or evidence that it left the country before the designation or at least 10 years before entry (19 CFR 12.104c); otherwise CBP seizes it

citations.label: State Department: current agreements and import restrictions
CBP ICP: Works of Art, Collector's Pieces, Antiques

rules.title: Stolen cultural property: an article documented in the inventory of a museum, religious or secular public monument or similar institution of a party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention and stolen from it after April 12, 1983 (or the later date the Convention took effect for that party) may not be imported

Iraq and Syria: archaeological and ethnological material illegally removed from Iraq since August 6, 1990 (19 CFR 12.104j) or unlawfully removed from Syria on or after March 15, 2011 (19 CFR 12.104k) is restricted under the designated lists of CBP Decisions 08-17 and 16-10

Pre-Columbian monumental or architectural sculpture and murals (stone carvings, stelae, architectural fragments, frescoes) first discovered in Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia or the Dominican Republic may not be imported without an export certificate from that country or proof it was exported on or before June 1, 1973

rules.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service / CBP
rules.title: Elephant ivory and other endangered-species parts: African elephant worked ivory may not be imported commercially (50 CFR 17.40(e)(5)), except antiques that meet the Endangered Species Act test: at least 100 years old, made of the species, not repaired or modified with endangered species parts since December 28, 1973, and entered through an antique port (Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Miami, San Juan, New Orleans, Houston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Anchorage, Honolulu or Chicago O'Hare) with FWS Form 3-177 (50 CFR 17.40(e)(9), 14.22; 19 CFR 10.53(e), 12.26). Scrimshaw is excluded, and CITES documents are still required

Wildlife items (ivory, tortoiseshell, rhinoceros horn, taxidermy, zoological specimens of 9705.22) must be declared to FWS on Form 3-177, enter at a designated port and be cleared before CBP releases them; CITES Appendix I items need a pre-Convention certificate or permits (50 CFR 23.45)

Invoices for works of art must say whether each work is an original, replica, reproduction or copy and name the artist; CBP may require the artist's or seller's declaration for sculptures and prints (19 CFR 10.48), and proof of age for antiques (19 CFR 10.53)

Merchandise processing fee: formal entries of Free art and antiques still pay 0.3464% of value, with a minimum of $34.58 and a maximum of $670.86 per entry from October 1, 2026 (fiscal year 2027); Chapter 98 entries are exempt

Report the Chapter 99 numbers with the Chapter 97 line: 9903.05.86 for the note 52(b) exemption from the 2026 Section 301 duty (and 9903.05.03 for Brazil), 9903.88.15 for China List 4A, 9903.03.14 for Canada's listed lines and 9903.90.08 for Russia

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 30, 50, 51 and 52

rules.title: Works lent from abroad for temporary, non-profit exhibition can be protected from seizure in U.S. courts if the State Department determines them to be of cultural significance and the exhibition in the national interest

groups.label: Paintings, drawings, pastels, collages & mosaics (executed by hand)
groups.note: Free. Wall paintings, mosaics and icons can be designated ethnological or archaeological material (for example Chinese wall art at least 250 years old, Greek and Cypriot ecclesiastical icons), and pre-Columbian murals are restricted. Normal frames go with the painting.

groups.label: Original engravings, prints & lithographs
groups.note: Free. Invoices should show the artist and that the prints were printed by hand from hand-made plates; photomechanical reproductions are heading 4911.

groups.label: Original sculptures & statuary, in any material
groups.note: Free, including the first 12 castings of a sculpture. Ancient and pre-Columbian sculpture is the main target of the cultural property rules; ivory carvings need the ESA antique test and an antique port.

groups.label: Postage & revenue stamps, first-day covers, postal stationery
groups.note: Free. Unused current-issue stamps are heading 4907. With de minimis suspended, even small stamp parcels need an entry; Canadian stamps pay 50%.

groups.label: Collections & collectors' pieces: archaeological, ethnographic, natural history, coins
groups.note: Free. Archaeological pieces and ancient coins (for example coins of Italian types) need export documents under the cultural property agreements; endangered-species specimens (9705.22) need FWS clearance.

groups.label: Antiques over 100 years old
groups.note: Free if over 100 years old, with proof of age; otherwise the article's normal rate plus 6.6%. Antiques with ivory, tortoiseshell or other endangered species enter only through an antique port with FWS Form 3-177.

faqs.question: Is art exempt from tariffs?
searchedAs: is art exempt from trump tariffs
is art exempt from us tariffs
is fine art exempt from tariffs
is original art exempt from us tariffs
are there tariffs on fine art
faqs.answer: Mostly yes. Every Chapter 97 line has a Free base rate, and the 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies exempt the whole chapter (U.S. note 52(b)), as does Brazil's 25% duty. In 2025–2026 the IEEPA tariffs and the Section 122 surcharge excepted paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps and collectors' pieces as informational materials (50 U.S.C. 1702(b)(3)); both have ended. Exceptions today: Chinese art pays 7.5%, many Canadian works 50% and Russian works 35%.

faqs.question: Are antiques subject to U.S. tariffs?
searchedAs: are antiques subject to us tariffs
faqs.answer: Antiques over 100 years old (9706) are Free and, since July 24, 2026, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. They were not exempt before: antiques are not informational materials, so they paid the IEEPA reciprocal duties from April 5, 2025 to February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge to July 23, 2026. Today only Chinese (7.5%), Russian (35%) and Canadian antiques 100–250 years old (50%) pay extra.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on art and antiques from the UK?
searchedAs: tariffs on art from uk to us
import duty on art from uk to usa
faqs.answer: No duty today. British paintings, sculptures, prints and antiques are Free: the UK's 10% 2026 Section 301 duty does not apply to Chapter 97 (note 52(b), report 9903.05.86). British antiques paid 10% from April 5, 2025 until July 23, 2026 (IEEPA, then Section 122); art did not. Expect the merchandise processing fee on formal entries, and UK export licensing for some cultural goods is a separate UK matter.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on art and antiques from France and Europe?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on antiques from europe
faqs.answer: No. EU art and antiques are Free: the EU's 10% floor under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.39) does not apply to Chapter 97. French, Italian and German antiques paid the EU's IEEPA rate (10%, then 15% all-in from August 7, 2025) until February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge until July 23, 2026. Italian archaeological material and coins of Italian types need Italian export documents.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on art from Canada?
searchedAs: tariffs on art from canada to us
are there tariffs on art from canada
are there tariffs on artwork from canada
faqs.answer: Yes, on many works. Since August 22, 2026, Canadian paintings and drawings (9701.21, 9701.91, 9701.99), recent original prints, all original sculptures, stamps, most collectors' pieces and antiques 100–250 years old pay a 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14), even with USMCA. Mosaics, prints over 100 years old, coins over 100 years old and antiques over 250 years old stay Free. Personal-use items in accompanied baggage and Chapter 98 temporary entries are not charged.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on art and antiques from China?
faqs.answer: 7.5% on every Chapter 97 line: the Section 301 List 4A duty (9903.88.15), which has no informational-materials exception; the product exclusions once granted for art and antiques have expired. The 2026 Section 301 duty does not apply. Chinese archaeological material through the Tang period and monumental sculpture and wall art at least 250 years old also need a Chinese export permit under the U.S.–China cultural property agreement.

faqs.question: How much is U.S. import duty on artwork?
searchedAs: import duty on artwork to usa
is there customs duty on artwork
faqs.answer: Zero for most origins: original paintings, drawings, prints and sculptures are Free (9701–9703). Formal entries (over $2,500) pay the merchandise processing fee, 0.3464% of value with a $34.58 minimum and $670.86 maximum from October 1, 2026. Chinese works pay 7.5%, Russian 35% and listed Canadian works 50%. Reproductions, posters and decorative articles are not Chapter 97 and pay their own rates plus the 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for paintings and artwork?
searchedAs: hs code for artwork on canvas
hs code for painting with frame
faqs.answer: Paintings, drawings and pastels executed entirely by hand are 9701: 9701.21 if over 100 years old, 9701.91 otherwise (mosaics 9701.22 / 9701.92, collages and similar 9701.29 / 9701.99). A frame of a normal kind and value is classified with the painting (note 6). Printed reproductions and art prints made photomechanically are 4911.91; original hand-pulled prints are 9702.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a sculpture?
faqs.answer: Original sculptures and statuary in any material are 9703: 9703.10 if over 100 years old, 9703.90 otherwise, Free. Heading 9703 includes the first 12 castings made from the sculptor's model (additional U.S. note 1). Mass-produced statuettes and works of conventional craftsmanship are classified by material, for example ceramic statuettes in 6913, wooden ones in 4420 and base-metal ones in 8306.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for antiques and antique furniture?
faqs.answer: Antiques over 100 years old are 9706: 9706.10 if over 250 years old, 9706.90 if 100–250 years, each with statistical suffixes for silverware (.20), furniture (.40) and other (.60), Free. Antique paintings, prints, sculptures, stamps and collectors' pieces stay in 9701–9705 (note 5(b)). Loose pearls and precious or semiprecious stones are never Chapter 97 (note 1(c)), and an article under 100 years old takes its normal heading.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for collectible coins and stamps?
faqs.answer: Coins of numismatic interest are 9705.31 (over 100 years old, with suffixes by age and gold or other) or 9705.39; non-legal-tender coins that are not collectors' pieces are 7118. Used stamps, first-day covers and unused stamps not of current issue are 9704.00.00; unused current-issue stamps are 4907. All are Free except from China (7.5%), Canada (50% on 9704 and 9705.39) and Russia (35%).

faqs.question: Can I import antiquities and archaeological objects into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the object is not restricted. Designated archaeological and ethnological material of the more than 30 countries with U.S. cultural property agreements or emergency actions (19 CFR 12.104g) needs the country's export certificate or proof it left before the designation or at least 10 years before entry. Material removed from Iraq since 1990 or Syria since 2011, stolen museum inventory and pre-Columbian monumental sculpture are restricted. CBP seizes restricted items.

faqs.question: Can you import ivory antiques into the U.S.?
searchedAs: can you import ivory into the us
faqs.answer: Only as a qualifying antique, or in narrow non-commercial cases. Commercial imports of African elephant worked ivory are banned (50 CFR 17.40(e)), but an antique at least 100 years old, not repaired with endangered species parts since December 28, 1973, may enter through one of 13 antique ports (such as New York, Boston, Los Angeles or Chicago O'Hare) with FWS Form 3-177 and its CITES documents. Scrimshaw does not qualify.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import art and antiques from?
faqs.answer: Mostly from Europe: France $2.87B, United Kingdom $1.63B, Italy $1.09B, Germany $1.03B, Spain $547M of the $9.98B imported in 2025 (up 12.2% from 2024). Paintings are the largest product. U.S. import statistics record the country of origin, so a French painting bought in London counts as French.
